title: Three speeches of Hamlet
where: *Hamlet*, Act 1, Scene 2; Act 3, Scene 1; Act 5, Scene 2
about: Hamlet, prince of Denmark, has come home from university after his father’s death and found his mother married to his uncle, who is now king. In the first passage he answers her before the court. His father’s ghost then tells him that the uncle was the murderer, and in the second passage, two acts later, the uncle still reigns and Hamlet is talking to himself. In the third, the King has rigged a fencing match to kill him, and his friend Horatio has just said he will put it off.

view.says: Auden wrote that Hamlet has no faith in God or in himself, so he can say who he is only through other people: the man whose uncle murdered his father and is married to his mother. He wishes to be what the hero of a Greek tragedy is, someone made by his situation. That is why he cannot act: he can only “act,” which Auden glosses as playing at possibilities.
view.quote: Hence his inability to act, for he can only “act,” i.e., play at possibilities.
view.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer's Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 21421-21436 (the page heads are at lines 21382 and 21433)

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: After the first line, one sentence runs for six lines and a half. It opens ’Tis not, so a denial is coming. Then it lists, a line to each, the cloak, the black suits, the sigh, the tears, the face, then all the rest, and four times nor brings in the next. What they cannot do comes only in the last five words: That can denote me truly. A verb kept to the end holds the sense open until every sign of mourning has been named. Two lines later Hamlet says what he does have and gives it no noun: that within.
lenses.why: The sentence lists every outward sign of grief, a line to each, before its last words say what they cannot do; a verb kept to the end holds the sense open until all are named.

grounds.claim: where the sentence runs, the list of signs, the four nors and the place of the verb
a sentence that keeps its main point to the end is not complete until then
grounds.source: Wikipedia, Periodic sentence

lenses.label: Naming
lenses.name: periphrasis
lenses.plain: the long way round: a description put in the place of a name
lenses.caption: Three lines are cut to one pattern: an adjective, a noun, then the breath, the eye or the face it belongs to. Hamlet does not say sigh, tears or sad face. He says suspiration, a word found in Shakespeare only here; a river in the eye; and the haviour, the bearing, of the visage. Rhetoric calls this periphrasis, the long way round. Each phrase names a sign by where it shows. Three lines on, the speech says what the signs are: actions that a man might play. In Act 2 Hamlet describes a player in tears by much the same signs: his visage, tears in his eyes, a broken voice.
lenses.why: Three signs of grief are named the long way round, by the breath, eye or face where each shows; the speech calls them actions a man might play, and Hamlet later describes a weeping player by much the same signs.

lenses.caption: The Queen has asked why, if death is common, it seems so particular with Hamlet. The verb could mean appears; he takes it as is so in appearance only. Three of his words for outward grief are also playhouse words. Actions are the gestures that go with speech; in Act 3 he tells the players to suit the action to the word. To play is to act a part. A show is a display, and also a stage spectacle, like the players’ dumb show, a scene acted without words. Trappings and suits are things put on. Auden’s account of Hamlet turns on a playhouse word with two senses: he cannot act, he can only “act.”
lenses.why: Hamlet’s words for the outward signs of grief are stage words: actions are gestures, to play is to act, a show is a spectacle; Auden’s account of him turns on the two senses of act.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Hamlet speaks blank verse, the unrhymed five-beat line, and for nine lines the line-ends do not rhyme. The last two do: show, woe. The quick return of a rhyme makes two lines felt as one closed unit. On Shakespeare’s stage a rhymed pair often marked a scene’s end: ten of this play’s twenty scenes end on one. The players’ play in Act 3 rhymes in pairs. Here a rhymed pair closes a speech in mid-scene, and the King answers. Seem comes three times, show twice, last as the rhyme. Hamlet has set himself apart from actions that a man might play. Auden, lecturing on the play in 1947, said that Hamlet is an actor and acts theatrically.
lenses.why: The speech is unrhymed until its last two lines; a rhymed pair was often the stage’s way of ending a scene, so the speech that sets Hamlet apart from playing closes on a closing device of the stage.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat, without rhyme; some lines run one unstressed syllable past the last beat

points.say: Two ways to say it: the stress on *that*, as marked here, or on *is*.
The eleventh syllable, unstressed: a weak ending.
An extra unstressed syllable before the pause in mid-line. The question ends here.
The first line of the speech to end on a beat.
The weak ending again, the fifth in these ten lines.
The line stops at the dash. *Ay* is then stressed where the line has no beat, between the beats on *dream* and *there’s*.

lenses.caption: The play’s verse line has ten syllables, every second one a beat, the last included. Five of the ten lines, the first four and the eighth, add an unstressed eleventh: a weak ending, which tends to give the line a falling rhythm, from stressed to unstressed. The question fills four such lines and stops inside the fifth, on another unstressed syllable, them. The sixth, eighth, ninth and tenth also stop inside the line. Auden said in 1947 that in Hamlet Shakespeare tries out the stop inside the line to make a voice between passion and prose. At ay a stress stands between two beats; stresses side by side slow the voice before there’s the rub.
lenses.why: Five lines run a syllable past the last beat, which tends to give a falling rhythm, and five stop inside the line; Auden said that in Hamlet Shakespeare tries out such stops to make a voice between passion and prose.

lenses.label: Verbs

spans.label: the only subject that is a person

lenses.caption: Twelve times in ten lines to is followed by a verb: to be, to die, to sleep. This is the infinitive, the form tied to no person: it names an act without its doer. Only six verbs have a subject: five forms of is, and we end. In thirty-three lines to himself Hamlet never says I, me or my; his six other long speeches to himself each say them at least seven times. In his 1947 lecture Auden said that this speech can be lifted out of the play and out of the character. He wrote that Hamlet cannot act, only play at possibilities. The thirty-three lines end on lose the name of action.
lenses.why: Twelve times in ten lines a verb comes as an infinitive, the form with no person, and in thirty-three lines Hamlet never says I; Auden said this speech can be lifted out of the character and the play.

lenses.label: Chain
lenses.name: anadiplosis
lenses.plain: a doubling back: the words that end one clause begin the next
lenses.caption: Twice Hamlet says to die, to sleep. The first time he adds No more, and the sentence goes on to what a sleep would end. The second time the line stops on sleep, and its last two words begin the next line. Rhetoric calls this anadiplosis: what ends one clause begins the next. The repeated word becomes the start of a further step. He has called death a sleep, and from sleep the next step is dreaming, perchance to dream. He says at once what that is: the rub. The next lines give the reason: the dreams that may come must give us pause.
lenses.why: The second time he says to die, to sleep, the last words begin the next line, and the repeated word leads one step on, to dream; the speech calls that step the rub that checks the wish.

grounds.claim: the words that end row 46.8 begin row 46.9; the first time, the phrase is followed by No more
anadiplosis: a line or phrase begins by repeating the word or words that ended the one before; it is often used to build to a climax
grounds.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, anadiplosis (n.); Wikipedia, Anadiplosis

notes.note: From French *outrage*, which goes back to Latin *ultra*, beyond: at root, a passing beyond bounds. English ears came to hear *rage* in it.

notes.note: A rub was an unevenness in the ground, and in bowls anything that slows a bowl or turns it from its course; so any obstacle.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, rub (n.); Schmidt, Shakespeare Lexicon, Rub (noun and verb); compare Richard II, Act 3, Scene 4, where the Queen is asked to play at bowls; Auden’s gloss to his class, spring 1947: Lectures on Shakespeare (2000), p. 327

lenses.caption: The question is asked in the words of a fight: slings, arrows, take arms, opposing. Shocks belongs with them: a shock was a violent collision, as of armies. Outrageous meant violent; it comes from the Latin for beyond and has no root in rage. Dying gets other words: sleep, end, and consummation, from the Latin for summing up and finishing. It is to be wished for devoutly, with devotion. The word that stops the wish is a term from the game of bowls, as Auden told his class in 1947. A rub is whatever slows the bowl or turns it from its course. The speech turns there, from the wish to the dread of what may come after death.
lenses.why: The question is put in a fight’s words and dying in words of rest and finishing; the word that stops the wish, rub, is a bowler’s word, as Auden told his class, for what turns the bowl from its course.

lenses.label: Crossing
lenses.name: antimetabole
lenses.plain: the same words said again in the opposite order
lenses.caption: Three clauses begin with if. The first sets now against not to come. The second says the same two things in the opposite order: not to come, then now. The third changes one term, not now, and ends it will come. Whichever case holds, it comes. The verb of the second passage, be, is here again, and now it has a time and a subject, it, which is never named. Auden wrote of the character as a whole that Hamlet wishes to be what the hero of a Greek tragedy is, someone made by his situation. In these clauses what is coming is the subject of every verb; the next sentence has a noun for its subject, readiness.
lenses.why: The two terms, now and to come, are said and then said again in the opposite order, so each case is tried and each ends the same: it comes; the subject of the next sentence is a noun, readiness.

grounds.claim: the order of now and not to come in the three clauses, and the subject it with its forms of be

lenses.caption: Horatio has told Hamlet to obey his misgiving. Augury was the Roman art of telling what is to come from signs, most often the flight of birds. Hamlet defies it: rejects it. His next sentence names a bird. The sparrow is the Gospel’s: in Matthew not one falls to the ground without the Father. Special providence is theology’s term for that care over each single thing. Calvin’s chapter on it infers from the sparrow that the flight of birds is ruled by God’s counsel. Hamlet refuses the art that reads birds for warnings, and goes from the bird whose fall is in God’s care to the three ifs.
lenses.why: Augury read what is to come most often from the flight of birds; Hamlet rejects it and at once names the Gospel’s bird, the sparrow whose fall is in God’s care: one sentence refuses omens and the next asserts providence.

grounds.claim: augury: the Roman augurs made the future known by watching lightning, the flight or notes of birds and other signs, and the kind that watched the flight of birds was the most common; in English the word’s first sense was foretelling from how birds fly
grounds.source: Lewis and Short, A Latin Dictionary, augur and augurium; Online Etymology Dictionary, augury (n.)

lenses.caption: In the first four acts Hamlet has seven long speeches to himself, of twelve to fifty-eight lines, all in verse. Auden wrote that the audience hears such a speech as spoken to them. In Act 5 Hamlet has none and is never alone on the stage. This speech about what is coming is five sentences of prose, said to Horatio. It is his last prose in this text: the court comes in and he speaks verse to the end. Auden said in 1947 that Hamlet speaks verse to himself and, when passion is high, to others; with other people he otherwise mostly speaks prose. By the count drawn here, about half of what he says to others is verse.
lenses.why: Hamlet’s seven long speeches to himself are all verse and all in Acts 1 to 4; this speech is prose, said to Horatio, and Auden said prose is what Hamlet mostly speaks with other people.

auden.says: In 1941, the year of the Michigan course, Auden talked about Shakespeare one evening at home with Charles Miller, a student in the class who shared his house. A director casting Hamlet, he said, might as well go into the street and take whoever comes first, because the part needs no actor. It is enough to say the speeches aloud: in them Hamlet is instructing himself, and arguing with himself, about how to act the parts he has decided to play.
auden.source: Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), p. 61

auden.says: Auden wrote that a whole personality, with what it discloses and what it hides, can hardly be shown through one character. The soliloquy tries to get round this, but it is a convention: it puts what is in fact a dialogue into the shape of one person’s speech. In Hamlet’s soliloquies the voice that is supposed to speak to itself is heard as speaking to the audience, who then suspect that he lets them hear only what he judges fit for them and keeps back the rest.
auden.quote: a single voice which is supposed to be addressed to himself but, in fact, is heard as addressed to us
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 110

auden.says: In *The Enchafèd Flood* Auden says that Shakespeare had a new idea of revenge and made of the Hamlet he inherited the earliest hero of the romantic kind. It is his situation that makes this Hamlet a hero: his mother’s adultery with the uncle who killed his father. Until then he was an ordinary, agreeable young man. So he does not simply avenge his father and have done with it. In secret he holds the situation dear and cannot bring himself to end it, because he would not know who he was without it.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), p. 110

auden.says: In his 1947 lecture on the play Auden cited T. S. Eliot’s verdict that it fails as a work of art, and said that Hamlet, the one character who does not act, is not well fitted into it. He doubted that anyone had played the part without looking ridiculous. It should be given, he said, to someone brought in from the street, with professionals in every other part, because Hamlet is an actor, and nobody can act himself. He called Hamlet bored at bottom, and said that is why he behaves theatrically.
auden.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), pp. 159 and 164

auden.says: In the same lecture Auden said that the soliloquies of *Hamlet*, like those of other plays Shakespeare wrote in those years, can be detached from the character and from the play; in his earlier and later plays they are more closely worked in. The speech of the second passage was his clear example. He also said that Hamlet is given verse when he is alone, in the soliloquies, and with others when passion is high, as with his mother, and that with other people he otherwise mostly speaks prose.
auden.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), pp. 159–60

auden.says: Also in that lecture Auden said that in *Hamlet* Shakespeare tries out the caesura, the stop inside the verse line, to get a voice between the passionate and the prosaic. He said too that Shakespeare’s paired adjectives change in this play: an earlier pair says one thing twice, and the pairs in *Hamlet* join an abstract word to a concrete one.

auden.says: In the spring of 1947 the Saturday class that went with Auden’s New York lectures on Shakespeare turned to language: close comment on single words and phrases of two plays, *Hamlet* and *The Tempest*. The final examination that term, as a student’s journal reports it, asked what single words in the two plays mean and had the students punctuate one of Hamlet’s prose speeches.
auden.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), Appendix I, pp. 321–40, and Appendix II, p. 341

auden.says: Alan Ansen’s notes of that class keep what Auden said on the speech of the second passage: *rub* is a bowler’s term, for a ball turned aside when it grazes another; editors have proposed changes to *sea of troubles*; and *to say*, two lines on, does not follow grammatically. The notes on *Hamlet* open with a general remark: Hamlet’s good relations with people all go bad, except the one with Horatio.

Counts made on the text printed here: the scenes that end on a rhymed pair; Hamlet’s lines and words of verse and of prose, scene by scene; his speeches to himself, and *I*, *me* and *my* in each. A word is what stands between spaces.
caveats: Auden’s 1947 lecture on *Hamlet* is not his own text. Arthur Kirsch rebuilt it from notes made by people who heard it. It was read here only in snippets of scanned copies of the book, and so were the notes of his 1947 class.
The remark of 1941 comes from a memoir that Charles Miller printed in 1983, forty-two years later. The memoir was read here only in snippets.

The stresses marked on the second passage are one reader’s hearing of the lines. Its first line can take a stress on *that* or on *is*, and a few other syllables could fairly be marked otherwise. The pauses marked follow the punctuation of the text printed here.

The text printed here reads *shows of grief* in the first passage, where the early editions called quartos read *shapes*. The counts of verse, prose and rhymed scene-endings follow this text, which sets a few short prose lines as verse.
Auden’s sentence that Hamlet has no faith in God is about the character as a whole. No remark of his was found on the first or the third passage, and in the third Hamlet speaks of providence.
open: No record was found of what Auden said about Hamlet in the Michigan class itself. One remark he made at home in 1941 was found by the examiner and added: Charles Miller’s memoir (1983), p. 61 by Kirsch’s note and by the page label of Google Books’ snippet of Miller’s book. It was seen only in snippets (archive.org full-text search, Google Books) of Miller’s book, of Kirsch’s note and of James Fenton’s The Strength of Poetry (2001). The view given here is from The Dyer’s Hand (1962); the research notes report that the same paragraph already stood in his essay “The Ironic Hero” in the late 1940s.

Auden’s 1947 lecture on Hamlet and Ansen’s notes of his 1947 class were read only in snippets of two scans of the book (archive.org full-text search; Google Books’ search within the volume) and in the research notes; no whole page was seen. The pages given (159, 159–60, 160, 164, 321–40, 324, 327, 381) are the page labels of the Google Books snippets (341, for the report of the spring examination, rests on the contents page alone), and agree with the contents page, the index and a running head seen in the archive.org snippets. A reader with the book should still check them, and should read the class notes on Hamlet (pp. 324–35) in full: only the lines of the three passages were searched.

The scan of The Enchafèd Flood loses the end of the sentence about Hamlet on p. 110. The examiner read the end in a snippet of another scan of the same edition and completed the paraphrase; the page number rests on the first scan.

Calvin’s phrase special providence was read in Beveridge’s English of 1845, not in the English translation of 1561 that Shakespeare’s contemporaries read. Two leads seen only in search snippets, neither used: Thomas Gataker’s Of the Nature and Use of Lots (1619) uses the phrase several times, once beside the sparrow; and books that print the early texts side by side show the First Quarto (1603) reading predestinate for special.
The text printed here reads shows of grief in the first passage; Schmidt’s lexicon notes that the quartos read shapes. A caveat now says so.
Rows 46.4 and 46.9 each hold two words joined by a dash. The marks that mean one of the two now name the part (6.1, 6.2, 4.1); the beat lens and one of its remarks still take the whole word.

Row 46.0 can be said with the stress on that or on is, row 46.3 with its first stress on Or or on take, and row 46.5 with No light or stressed. In row 46.6 natural is taken as two syllables. In row 46.9 there’s can be said with or without a stress; the caption rests on ay alone. No caption leans on the doubtful syllables.
The count of ten scenes that end on a rhymed pair includes move and love at the end of Act 2, Scene 1, which today rhyme to the eye only.
The hosted text sets a few short prose lines as verse, so the counts of Hamlet’s verse and prose by scene, and the statement that this is his last speech in prose, are as that text sets them.

The lead on hendiadys was not made a lens. The published count of the figure in Hamlet (George T. Wright, PMLA 96, 1981: perhaps sixty-six) was seen only in its abstract, and a report of its list implies that the pair in the first passage, trappings and suits, is not on it. Auden named hendiadys to his 1947 class in a list of terms (Lectures on Shakespeare, p. 323, snippet), and his lecture speaks of paired adjectives in Hamlet (p. 160, now in the list of what he said); neither remark is about these passages.

The third passage has Hamlet speak of providence, and the view says he lacks faith in God. No remark of Auden’s on that speech, or on the first passage, was found in the scans or in the scanned lectures (searched by phrase), or in Ansen’s notes of the 1947 class as the snippets show them. A caveat says so.

Auden’s lecture says that Hamlet mostly speaks prose with other people. The count bears out half of it: all seven long speeches to himself are verse and nearly all his prose is said to others (one aside of fifteen words in Act 2, Scene 2 is prose), but in Act 1 he speaks verse only, and over the play he says about as many words of verse to others as of prose (4,894 and 4,904 by the count; 3,547 of verse without the scene with his mother, which Auden excepts). Since the finisher’s change of 3 October the Shape caption reports the remark and then says, in a sentence of its own, that by the count about half of what he says to others is verse; it claims no more. The finisher counted again with remake/works/hamlet/finisher/count-others.py: the same figures, and 4,883 of verse beside 4,889 of prose if the three asides are taken out as well.

The poet’s mark on row 46.5 (words 0 to 1) in the Chain tab was removed by the examiner: the tab had six kinds of mark, and its label was a gloss with no ground. If it is wanted back it needs a tag of its own, since the chain drawing links marks that share a tag.

The Beat tab has new pause marks on rows 46.4, 46.5, 46.7 and 46.8; the stop in row 46.9 falls at the dash inside a joined word, where the beat lens cannot draw a pause, and a remark on that row says so. The artist has looked (art.md, section 4, the first thing still there): the kit must learn to draw a pause at a dash inside a joined word, and the lead has that; the marks of row 46.9 are as they were.

Ansen’s notes also record that Auden called to say in row 46.5 a grammatical difficulty and noted emendations of sea of troubles in row 46.3. Both are in the list of what he said; no tab uses them. The Verbs tab could.

Appendix III of Lectures on Shakespeare (pp. 347–62) lists the lines Auden marked in his own copy of Hamlet. The snippets of that list were too broken to tell whether the lines of the three passages are among them. Someone with the book should look.

The list of what Auden said had five entries when the poet handed it in and twelve after the examiner. The lead took out three that mention Hamlet only in passing, in essays on other subjects (Forewords and Afterwords, p. 228; The Dyer’s Hand, pp. 241 and 408). The critic took out a fourth (The Enchafèd Flood, pp. 34 and 102), so the list has eight, and the finisher put the remark of 1941, the one entry from the year of the course, first. The four taken out are kept at the end of notes.md, before the finisher’s record.
